articles.title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The asymptotic error of representational similarity metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) has been well-characterized, but there are no realistic bounds on how estimates of representational similarity $\textit{simultaneously}$ depend on the number of sampled neurons ($N$) and experimental conditions ($M$). We study the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, which we call the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD). We show that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, whereas several popular similarity measures including CKA have no unbiased estimator. Under mild assumptions, we show that estimation error of CKD decays in proportion to $1/M + 1/N$. Strikingly, the rate in this bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions. Thus, similarity estimation does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which plagues similar problems in high-dimensional statistics. We verify our results empirically in random shallow neural networks, trained neural networks, and macaque visual cortex data. Ultimately, this paper advances a framework for predicting the error of similarity estimators in experiments by relaxing existing, biologically-unrealistic assumptions. Our theoretical and empirical predictions produce specific prescriptions on how to most efficiently estimate the similarity between multiple neural systems.

articles.title: A Realistic End-to-End Runtime Crossover Estimation for Quantum-Enhanced Training of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33454v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is one promising application domain for Quantum Computing (QC) speedups, but asymptotic complexity considerations often mask the actual engineering costs of actual end-to-end workflows. For the use case of training a linearized Neural Network with a Quantum Linear Solver, a provably favorable quantum scaling has been suggested. We present realistic resource estimates for this problem, accounting for data access, computation, and readout. Our analysis examines three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios, under distinct sparsity-scaling assumptions, thereby enabling progressively more realistic resource estimates. We identify crossover regimes relative to classical methods and find that crossover points emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements. This work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML algorithms under realistic hardware constraints and help identifying the bottlenecks that must be overcome to approach industrial quantum utility.

articles.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the

articles.title: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.

articles.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33468v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.

articles.title: Memory as the Backbone: A Dual-Store Associative Memory Architecture for Visual Recognition
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate whether explicit memory can serve as the organizing principle of a general-purpose visual backbone. Inspired by the interaction between working and long-term memory in human cognition, we introduce DuSAM (Dual-Store Associative Memory), a hierarchical memory-native visual backbone coupling image-local working memory (WM) with a fixed-capacity persistent semantic memory (PM). WM organizes local visual evidence into compact, spatially anchored states that are updated and transported across stages, then read back to refine dense features. PM consolidates semantic evidence from training images and annotated regions into prototypes, whose retrieved content enriches the same working states. With these memory operations in place of self-attention or state-space blocks, DuSAM achieves competitive performance relative to representative, similarly sized backbones on ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and COCO object detection and instance segmentation. Ablations show contributions from both stores, with PM particularly benefiting class groups with fewer annotated training pixels. At $2048\times2048$, the complete DuSAM-based UPerNet segmentor achieves $2.36\times$ the throughput of the evaluated DeiT-S/16 counterpart while using $59.5\%$ less GPU memory, and $1.24\times$ the throughput of the linear-complexity VMamba-T. Memory analyses reveal spatially selective WM access and semantic associations between retrieved prototypes and training regions. Class-targeted removal and restoration further demonstrate that category-specific experience can be replenished through state updates without changing network parameters. These results establish explicit memory as a viable organizing principle for visu

articles.title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.

articles.title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33489v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Without data, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in continuous time have so far failed to develop vortex shedding past a circular cylinder in a domain symmetric about the wake centerline: the training converges to the steady symmetric solution. We obtain shedding at Re=100 with a continuous-time PINN trained over successive time windows, without any reference data and without temporal discretization, the symmetry being broken by an analytical, divergence-free initial condition. The Strouhal number and the mean drag coefficient agree with an OpenFOAM solution computed on the same domain to within 0.5%. The pressure, however, is discontinuous at the junctions between windows, and the lift coefficient is a staircase. We relate this discontinuity to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, of index 2 after spatial discretization: a consistent initial condition of each window must satisfy the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for the velocity, and the hidden constraint $\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0$, with $\partial_t\mathbf{v}$ given by the momentum equation, then determines the pressure. Imposing the pressure alone makes the solution continuous but not consistent; our remedy imposes the pressure at the junctions and adds this hidden constraint to the loss. Over five shedding periods, the jumps of the lift coefficient become 20 times smaller.

articles.title: Model Predictive Control of a Multirotor UAV with a Cable-Suspended Payload: A Comparison of Shifted and Transformer-Based Warm Starts
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33514v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study investigates model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor drone (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload, comparing conventional shifted initialization with Transformer-based warm starting of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The controller uses a coupled mechanical model with an elastic cable and a double-pendulum representation of the suspended load. Its formulation includes move-blocked control inputs, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and input-feasibility projection. A Transformer trained on expert SCP solutions predicts an initial control sequence, which is subsequently refined by the same optimizer used for the conventional methods. Numerical experiments compare zero, shifted, and Transformer initialization under identical controller settings. For independently solved MPC problems, Transformer initialization reduces computation time relative to zero initialization. In sequential closed-loop simulations, however, shifting the preceding optimized control sequence provides the lowest computation time, while all three methods produce similar tracking behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of comparing learned warm starts with conventional initialization methods that reuse previous MPC solutions. The measured optimization times exceed the control sampling period; consequently, real-time implementation is not demonstrated. Keywords: Model predictive control; sequential convex programming; Transformer; warm start; cable-suspended payload; multirotor drone.

articles.title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33531v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study adversarial bandit convex optimization, where in each of $n$ rounds a learner chooses a point $A_t$ in a convex body $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and observes only a noisy value of a convex loss $f_t:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$ at that point. The losses are chosen by an adversary, who may change them from round to round and adapt them to the learner's past actions. We improve the best known regret bound for this problem from $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ (Lattimore, 2020, 2026) to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, which matches the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). Together with the recent lower bound of $\Omega(d^{4/3}\sqrt n)$ due to Rajaraman and Han (2026), it determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$ and logarithmic factors. The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration. Unlike earlier methods of this kind, it uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian smoothing of the loss, rather than of an optimistic surrogate.

articles.title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33549v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.

articles.title: Symmetry-Aware Residual Learning of Few-Body Molecular Wave Functions
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33576v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ultracold polar molecules are a highly controllable platform for engineering quantum matter, but modeling their few-body properties remains computationally challenging. Their anisotropic long-range interactions and rich internal structure lead to high-dimensional eigenvalue problems for which conventional grid-based solvers are largely restricted to two-molecule systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a physics-informed neural variational method that exploits known physical structure of the molecular wave function. Our key idea is to factor the wave function into analytic and neural components. The analytic component encodes rotational symmetry and asymptotic decay, while the neural residual learns the remaining intermediate-range behavior. This decomposition reduces the effective dimensionality of the problem without relying on ad hoc approximations or problem-specific discretization grids. We benchmark our method against high-accuracy two-molecule solvers and recover both ground and excited bound states with mean relative errors below 0.01%. We further demonstrate the method's applicability to three-body systems by computing field-linked trimer ground-state energies in percent-level agreement with an independent grid-based calculation. This provides a systematic route to larger molecular systems and opens opportunities to study correlations and dynamics in interacting quantum matter.

articles.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33592v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-\gamma)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $\delta\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

articles.title: Interpreting Speckle Effects Through Neuron Interventions
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33632v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, reduces the performance of pretrained SAR models. We use interpretability methods to examine its effects inside pretrained vision models. We identify neurons that respond selectively to speckle and test whether correcting their activations improves reconstruction. We study SARMAE, an Earth observation model pretrained on a million-scale SAR dataset. Synthetic scenes with known reflectivity allow us to measure recovery precisely. The model contains 38 speckle-selective neurons that track speckle's value distribution. Restoring these neurons to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching across layers shows that the first MLP has the largest restoration and injection effects. Within this layer, a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1\% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes. When the speckle-selective neurons are held at their noisy values, 96.5\% of this gain remains, while holding the values of three decoder heads removes 37.4\%. In an ImageNet-pretrained MAE, restoration is most effective in the third MLP block. On manipulated Sentinel-1 and Capella images, the same 64 neurons also improve reconstruction, whereas for land-cover classification, only restoring the entire first MLP yields a clear gain. The neurons that respond most to speckle are therefore not the ones the model uses to recover the scene.

articles.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.

articles.title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences.

articles.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33672v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.

articles.title: Nepali Currency Denomination Classification Using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and MobileNetV2: An Experimental Comparison
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated currency denomination recognition is a computer vision task with applications in cash handling, financial technology, and assistive systems. This study classifies seven Nepali currency denominations (Rs. 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 500, and 1,000) using three configurations: a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN), MobileNetV2 with transfer learning, and MobileNetV2 with hyperparameter tuning. A compiled dataset of 16,249 images was used, comprising 10,500 training, 3,500 validation, and 2,249 independent test images. Images were resized to 128 x 128 pixels, normalized, and augmented to vary orientation, scale, illumination, and appearance. Models were evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and precision-recall and ROC analysis. The hyperparameter-tuned MobileNetV2 achieved the highest validation accuracy (95\%), with precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.93, 0.91, and 0.92, but reached only 84\% accuracy on the held-out test set. MobileNetV2 with transfer learning but no additional tuning achieved 89\% test accuracy, and the conventional CNN achieved 85\%. Transfer learning therefore provided a competitive approach under the evaluated conditions, while higher validation accuracy from tuning did not yield higher test accuracy. To demonstrate practical deployment, a Flask-based web prototype using TensorFlow Lite was developed, supporting image upload and live webcam recognition with both visual and voice output. The study shows the feasibility of combining lightweight deep learning with a voice-assisted web interface for Nepali currency recognition, and highlights the need for more diverse datasets, greater robustness under uncontrolled imaging conditions, and broader real-world evaluation.

articles.title: OrbACE: Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33743v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate electronic-structure reference data are expensive, motivating interatomic potentials that learn effectively from limited training sets. We introduce OrbACE (Orbital and Atomic Cluster Expansion), a framework that supplements an E(3)-equivariant cluster-expansion backbone with inexpensive electronic-structure descriptors. On ANI-1x at the $\omega$B97X/6-31G* level, its atom-centered variant, OrbACE-A, trained on 10,000 configurations and evaluated on 442,000 held-out configurations, achieves energy and force mean absolute errors of 3.16 meV/atom and 76 meV/angstrom in direct learning, compared with 9.61 meV/atom and 146 meV/angstrom for MACE with matched backbone settings. This reduces the energy error by a factor of three and approximately halves the force error. Its energy error is also below that of the best delta-corrected MACE baseline, 5.00 meV/atom, although its force error is slightly higher. Combining OrbACE-A with a Hartree-Fock delta baseline further reduces the errors to 1.48 meV/atom and 35 meV/angstrom. OrbACE-A builds atom- and pair-resolved invariants from a non-self-consistent extended-Hueckel model evaluated within the differentiable forward pass, yielding forces consistent with the predicted energy. The orbital variant, OrbACE-O, instead uses localized Hartree-Fock orbitals as graph nodes, with scalar and equivariant electronic descriptors. Its forces are evaluated at fixed descriptors, omitting their response to nuclear motion. In direct learning on ANI-1x, its energy error is approximately three times that of OrbACE-A. The three benchmarks considered (ANI-1x, revised MD17, and 3BPA) cover neutral, closed-shell, non-periodic molecules containing H, C, N, and O. Performance outside this domain

articles.title: Confidence-Based Adaptive Retrieval Fails Where It Matters Most: A Paradox in Biomedical Question Answering
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for biomedical question answering, but plausible incorrect answers remain a safety risk in clinical settings. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can ground responses in medical literature, while confidence-based adaptive RAG retrieves only when the model appears uncertain. We evaluate this routing strategy on three biomedical QA benchmarks of increasing difficulty and compare models across a broad range of parameter scales. The results reveal a paradox: confidence is well calibrated (AUROC 0.78--0.89) on standard medical exam questions where retrieval adds little value (+2.4\% to -1.4\%), yet becomes \emph{near-random} (AUROC 0.506) on specialist-level questions where retrieval helps most (+11.2\%). Five uncertainty signals---first-token probability, margin, entropy, consistency-based sampling, and verbalized confidence---show the same failure pattern. Five post-hoc calibration correction strategies, including density-ratio reweighting and rank-preserving transformation, do not recover a useful routing signal on hard questions (best AUROC: 0.507). Cross-model comparison shows that larger parameter scale and higher base accuracy do not guarantee reliable confidence-based routing under specialist-domain difficulty shift. These findings challenge the premise of confidence-based adaptive RAG: in high-stakes biomedical settings, defaulting to always-retrieve is safer and more accurate than confidence-based routing when calibration on the target domain is unknown.

articles.title: A comprehensive survey of deep face verification systems adversarial attacks and defense strategies
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Face Verification (FV) systems have exhibited remarkable performance in verification tasks and have consequently garnered extensive adoption across various applications, from identity duplication to authentication in mobile payments. However, the surge in popularity of face verification has raised concerns about potential vulnerabilities in the face of adversarial attacks. These concerns originate from the fact that advanced FV systems, which rely on deep neural networks, have recently demonstrated susceptibility to crafted input samples known as adversarial examples. Although imperceptible to human observers, adversarial examples can deceive deep neural networks during the testing and deployment phases. These vulnerabilities raised significant concerns about the deployment of deep neural networks in safety-critical contexts, prompting extensive investigations into adversarial attacks and corresponding defense strategies. This comprehensive survey provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in deep face verification, encompassing a broad spectrum of topics such as algorithmic designs, database utilization, protocols, and application scenarios. Furthermore, we conduct an in-depth examination of state-of-the-art algorithms to generate adversarial examples and the defense mechanisms devised to mitigate such adversarial threats.

articles.title: CriticalScenes: Scalable Photorealistic Critical-Scenario Generation for Closed-Loop Driving Adaptation
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety-critical interactions are rare in recorded driving data, leaving end-to-end driving planners with limited exposure to evasive behaviour during training. This lack of critical supervision can lead to unsafe behaviour and, in rare instances, collisions. To address this gap, we introduce CriticalScenes, a reconstruction-based framework that transforms ordinary recorded driving scenes into photorealistic safety-critical interactions with corresponding collision-avoidance supervision. Across 53 reconstructed source scenes, 979 of 1,060 attempted interactions yield feasible threat trajectories (92.4\%), while the inserted threat actors remain detectable in more than 95\% of non-occluded observations within 5--35\,m. Experiments with two structurally different end-to-end planners show that the generated supervision improves critical-scenario planning, while closed-loop transfer varies across planner architectures. SparseDrive achieves a 46.5\% relative reduction in collision rate on an independent photorealistic closed-loop benchmark, whereas UniAD shows only a modest closed-loop improvement despite substantial open-loop gains. The results further highlight the importance of closed-loop evaluation, as improvements in open-loop trajectory prediction do not necessarily translate into equivalent safety gains.

articles.title: CoSMo: A Compact Spectral Space of Body Motion in Video
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce CoSMo, a compact spectral space of body motion in video, in which each motion is a single code that can be compared and edited without training, transferred to a new subject, interpolated, composed, scaled in intensity and detail, or sampled anew. Our encoder expresses how a clip's DINOv2 features change over time in a fixed temporal basis, the discrete cosine transform (DCT), and compresses this change into 384 numbers. Because each frequency band is the same cosine pattern in every code, codes are aligned in time, ordered from coarse to fine, and can be blended or added without matching frames. What stays constant over a clip cancels, and keeping fewer frequencies leaves less of the performer and scene. The encoder is trained on real videos and on synthetic motions of several characters, and lightweight adapters let a frozen image-to-video model render any code with any subject. On unseen videos, our code ranks the same motion on other bodies higher than DisMo, a per-frame representation, while its nearest neighbors show the same performer about 40% less often with a seven times more compact code. In generation, without per-motion training, CoSMo transfers motion more faithfully than FlexiAct and a text-prompt baseline, at least as faithfully as DisMo on automatic metrics and clearly better between humanoid bodies, and its blends keep much more of both source motions than DisMo's. Users rank CoSMo first nearly twice as often as DisMo for motion transfer (59% vs. 30%), place it top-two 94% of the time, and prefer it in 76% of the interpolation comparisons.

articles.title: StyleID++: Position-Decoupled and Structure-Coherent Style Retrieval across Diffusion Architectures
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33323v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention injection offers a remarkably simple route to training-free style transfer: content queries retrieve style keys and values inside a pretrained diffusion model. We show that this operation also creates an overlooked failure mode. Position signals that are useful within one image become a spurious shared coordinate system across two spatially unrelated images, causing content tokens to favor style tokens at similar coordinates. This cross-image positional leakage appears in both convolutional U-Nets and diffusion transformers (DiTs), despite their different position mechanisms. Removing the positional shortcut exposes a second problem: unconstrained global retrieval lets related content tokens select incompatible style regions, producing fragmented appearance. We present StyleID++, a training-free framework that addresses the two problems jointly. Position-Decoupled Retrieval reduces coordinate-dependent matching through circular padding in U-Nets and injection-only RoPE removal in DiTs, while preserving native position modeling elsewhere. Affinity-Coherent Refinement then regularizes style assignments with the content self-attention graph, encouraging structurally related tokens to retrieve compatible style evidence. We quantify the leakage with a coordinate--centroid correlation and a permutation test on the style reference. The permutation error can be driven to zero in both backbones, which identifies the position mechanism as the carrier of the leakage, and StyleID++ obtains the best ArtFID of all methods we compare.

articles.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33339v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.

articles.title: LGCount: Layout-Guided Diffusion for Zero-Shot Object Counting
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Class-agnostic counting requires the user to specify what to count, usually with a class name or a few annotated boxes. We propose a richer text-based specification: a structured layout that names the target, the region that holds it, the distractors to ignore. A prompt upsampler writes this layout from the image and the requested category alone, and an image-editing diffusion model, adapted into a single-step counter, turns it into a density map. Because counting datasets pair each image with a single valid density map, a counter trained on it learns to ignore the layout. We therefore train on synthetic counterfactuals in which one image admits several valid density maps, so that the layout cannot be ignored. On FSC-147 we improve on the previous zero-shot state of the art and we set the best reported result on LOOKALIKES while being told the least about each image. A single photograph can be counted by category, by region, or by granularity without retraining.

articles.title: DDxBasis: Explaining Frozen Foundation Encoder-based Medical Classification by Exact Differential Diagnosis
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In differential diagnosis (DDx), a clinician explains a diagnosis by the few findings that separate it from the alternatives. Medical image classifiers cannot yet explain themselves this way. Existing explanations are either faithful but spread over hundreds of concepts, or compact but leave part of each decision unexplained. We present DDxBasis, which explains a classifier on a frozen foundation encoder as a differential diagnosis in three steps. First, a concept bottleneck reads all patch tokens at every encoder layer using gated, second-order slot attention. A concept basis then regroups the concepts into two-pole axes, each a differential between groups of diagnoses. Finally, we read a differential diagnosis from each axis through the typical presentation of its poles, the pertinent findings of the case, and counterfactual edits of borderline cases. Across five medical datasets, DDxBasis is the most accurate frozen-encoder model and close to the best published domain-specific results. Because every concept adds its own evidence, its reproducible concept basis splits each decision exactly, at no cost in accuracy. Without ordered stage or concept labels, the axes recover cell lineages and rare subtypes, agree with dermatologists' structure annotations, and expose planted and real shortcuts.

articles.title: Searching Ultra-Long Videos with Decision Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding ultra-long videos requires retrieving sparse, query-relevant evidence from extensive video histories. Existing similarity-based retrieval methods are efficient, but they encode the question and the video content independently and thus often miss evidence whose relevance requires reasoning over both. Generative large language models (LLMs) can perform such reasoning, but they typically generate text over multiple rounds of search, which makes each query slow and costly. In this work, we introduce DeLoVi (Decision Models for Long Video), a framework that leverages pretrained decision models to retrieve evidence from ultra-long videos. Like an LLM, a decision model reads the question together with the candidate evidence, so it can reason over both. Unlike an LLM, it directly outputs a relevance score without generating text, which makes it fast and inexpensive. We first present DeLoVi-S, a simple method that generates captions for short video clips and uses a decision model to rank those captions by their relevance to a question. A generative LLM then answers the question using the top-ranked captions. Despite its simplicity, DeLoVi-S achieves state-of-the-art performance on three ultra-long video understanding benchmarks, EgoLifeQA, EgoMemReason, and MM-Lifelong, and generalizes effectively to long-video understanding benchmarks, VideoMME-L and LVBench. However, DeLoVi-S scores every caption for every question, so its cost grows linearly with video length. To reduce this cost, we propose an automated policy evolution framework that iteratively refines the memory construction and retrieval policies around a fixed pretrained decision model. articles.title: MotifFlow: Training-Free, Self-Contained Style Transfer from Color to Motif in Rectified Flow Transformers
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Expressive style transfer must reproduce a painting's palette, brushwork, and characteristic motifs while retaining the content image's structure. Attention injection is effective in U-Net-based diffusion models, but adapting it to FLUX often transfers color without capturing the style's distinctive brushwork. Our analysis across backbones links this gap to how injected features are integrated across neighboring spatial locations. We introduce MotifFlow, a training-free, self-contained framework that combines style injection with style-alignment guidance in FLUX. Injection supplies style features during generation but does not explicitly encourage the model's native attention output to align with them. We therefore use the discrepancy between native and injected attention outputs to guide latent-space updates, encouraging the evolving image to develop the style's distinctive brushwork and motifs. Style encoding, guidance, and synthesis all use the same frozen backbone, without auxiliary image encoders or trained adapters. A single strength parameter controls the transition from color transfer to pronounced brushwork and motifs, with additional support for regional stylization and style mixing. Experiments on 1,000 content-style pairs show that MotifFlow better matches the local textures of the style image than baseline methods and produces more consistent stylization than injection alone. The same design extends to FLUX.2.

articles.title: VersionGS: Compact and Motion-Robust Dynamic Gaussian Splatting via Versioned Gaussians
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33374v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent dynamic Gaussian splatting methods encode temporal change, either as smooth functions of time or as constrained updates between frames. We observe that their reconstruction quality degrades significantly under fast motion. In challenging dance sequences, their PSNR drops by 1.1-4.0 dB on high-motion frames compared to low-motion frames. To overcome this limitation, we propose VersionGS, a method that directly encodes per-frame Gaussian states and uses motion estimation only to guide reconstruction. Within each group of frames, unchanged Gaussians keep their current versions in a shared dictionary, while modified Gaussians are appended as new versions. To maximize version reuse, we introduce selective sequential construction, which refines the Gaussians selected by optical flow, photograph differences or rendering errors and leaves the others unchanged. The dictionary is then pruned, fine-tuned with simulated quantization and encoded as images. Adjusting the pruning ratio trades off storage and quality without rebuilding the dictionary. On the fast dance sequences of DanceNet3D, VersionGS improves foreground PSNR by 2.7 dB over the best baseline, and its PSNR decreases by less than 0.3 dB on the highest-motion frames. On N3DV and Technicolor, it requires 6.0x and 5.7x less storage than TAD-GS, the strongest baseline overall, while achieving even higher PSNR. Finally, playback is fast and requires no motion model or neural network, only a 3DGS rasterizer.

articles.title: DreamTour: Layout Steering for Training-Free World Exploration
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video diffusion and world models generate plausible videos but do not reliably match the requested camera direction and travel distance. We present DreamTour, a training-free framework that generates camera tours from a single image with more accurate control over camera motion. DreamTour first uses a frozen image inpainting prior to extend the photograph beyond its original field of view while preserving the input pixels. Depth-based rendering of this extended scene along the requested camera path produces approximate target views that serve as spatial guidance. We introduce Layout Steering, which aligns early video latents with these views through decaying low-frequency corrections, leaving later denoising to refine appearance and dynamics. For longer tours, we autoregressively generate the video segments, repeating guidance construction from each segment's final frame to maintain camera control across the full trajectory. DreamTour improves directional accuracy and travel calibration on VBench while maintaining competitive video quality. On WorldScore, it strengthens camera control and scene consistency across chained movements. Together, these results demonstrate that training-free spatial guidance enables more accurate and consistent camera control in pretrained video diffusion and world models.

articles.title: ArtTet: Watertight Part Meshes of Articulated Objects from Rigid-Body Rules and Partitioned Marching Tetrahedra
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33382v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present ArtTet, a method that reconstructs an articulated object from multi-view observations of two articulation states and outputs one watertight mesh per rigid part together with the joints that move them. Mesh splatting gives explicit triangles, but it treats the object as one scene. It extracts a single global surface and cannot keep the triangles of different parts apart; the mesh it exports is layered, self-intersecting, and full of holes. ArtTet follows a divide-and-conquer strategy instead. We first divide the object into rigid parts with dynamic- and geometric-constrained articulation and ownership inference. A multibody registration of the two states recovers the parts and their screw joints. Rigid-body rules on attachment, contact, and swept motion then correct joint types and part labels without any part annotation. We then divide space into part cells with an articulated tetrahedral partition, and conquer each cell with its own differentiable signed distance field on a shared tetrahedral grid. In these partitioned marching tetrahedra the fields are mutually exclusive by construction, so the extracted part meshes are closed and never overlap. All part meshes are optimized jointly from the images of both states through the recovered joints. On Articulate-100, ArtTet gives the most accurate axis directions, part motions, and part geometry over all objects among methods that use no part masks, and its part meshes have virtually no open boundary edges. We also show reconstructions of real captures from the SplArt dataset.

articles.title: Synchronizing Cameras via 3D Object Relationships
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we synchronize multiple videos of the same dynamic event through object relationships. Driven by dynamic reconstruction and novel view synthesis, many recent synchronization methods rely on pixel-level evidence, such as point correspondences across views or the photometric losses of a reconstructed scene. In dynamic scenes, however, fast motion and occlusions make the moving regions that carry much of the timing information hard to match across views. We thus propose to bring back the traditional wisdom that objects are reliable cues for global reasoning about cameras. Measured in 3D, the relationships between objects, such as the distance between two people, are stable across all views up to scale; they can serve as cues for alignment. To compare these relationships across cameras, we only need the identity of each object in every view, as the cues are relational. We obtain these identities by giving a vision-language model a few frames of every camera and prompting it to identify the objects in the scene. We then segment and track each identified object through every video with an open-vocabulary segmentor. To obtain the 3D locations of objects, we use a pretrained depth estimator. Where depth or segmentation fails, we complement these 3D cues with 2D motion from point tracks. Finally, we synchronize the cameras by finding the temporal offsets at which the cues of different cameras agree best, first for each camera pair and then for all cameras jointly with robust optimization. We evaluate our method on four standard benchmarks, outperforming the state of the art.

articles.title: Measuring and Predicting Image-Token Repair Boundaries in Vision-Language Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33388v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Degraded images make vision-language models answer wrongly. Using synthetic paired blur, noise, and low light, we trace which clean image states can still repair those answers from the vision encoder through the language model. In four encoder models, 12 to 23 ranked tokens recover half of the full-patch effect, whereas random orders require four to fifteen times as many; encoder-free Gemma needs 22.2 versus 53.1. Full-block repair expires at a model-specific language-model crossing. The matched reverse-direction intervention is algebraically identical to text-token restoration, so its gap from image restoration measures a redundancy band rather than an independent predictor. A clean-image gray-ablation crossing independently predicts held-out repair with 1.53-layer error, against 3.65 for shared depth. Gemma MMBench has the only large attention-to-repair point gap; Gemma GQA does not. Restormer provides a non-oracle consistency check on two models.

articles.title: BreathSplat: Grounding One Smooth Motion in the Breathing Phase for 4D Cone-Beam CT
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Four-dimensional cone-beam computed tomography (4D-CBCT) images the anatomy of a breathing patient, but sees each breathing phase from only a few angles. Breathing, however, is a smooth motion that repeats; it has a phase. Existing methods exploit this either by reconstructing the anatomy as a function of the breathing phase, often through bins, or by estimating smooth dynamic motions in time. Yet none of these grounds one smooth motion in the phase. We thus propose to share projections across breathing phases with splines. Specifically, we represent the 4D volume with dynamic Gaussians whose motion uses B-splines in space and time. We ground the motion state in the respiratory phase, which we read from well-studied conventional surrogates. Projections at the same phase in different breathing cycles then constrain the same anatomy and motion. On simulated lung scans, our method, BreathSplat, outperforms recent dynamic methods in reconstruction and motion accuracy, including those given the ground-truth phase. We further show qualitatively, on two real patient scans, that our method provides clearer reconstructions than the state of the art.

articles.title: ArtKit: Motion-Driven Re-Segmentation and Link Re-Generation for Articulated Objects from RGB-D Video
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An RGB-D camera that films an object being moved, often from one viewpoint, sees one side of it and how its parts move. We present ArtKit, which takes such a video as input to create an articulated model with complete parts, a kinematic tree, and typed joints. Our central idea is generating the hidden geometry and verifying it against what the camera sees. A generative part prior proposes complete, part-decomposed geometry based on the first frame. Point tracks, grouped into rigid trajectories, split and merge the generated parts into links. We then fit revolute and prismatic joints, with a visibility-aware energy ensuring that the articulated model explains the depth observed across the video. A rule checks against the video to choose between synchronous group fits and per-frame chain fits, so that one pipeline serves a diverse range of articulated objects, such as household items and robotic hands. Finally, we regenerate each link of the chosen fit as one part and keep it wherever it agrees better with the observations. We evaluate on Articulate-100 and on HArt, a new benchmark of 60 PartNet-Mobility objects and 8 robotic hands and grippers rendered as RGB-D videos with ground-truth parts and joints. ArtKit reduces the axis and part motion errors of the strongest baseline by more than half on the objects, as well as the axis error on the hands. ArtKit also runs on real recordings and generated videos.

articles.title: Beyond Random Starts: Amortized Initialization for Adversarial Attacks on Vision-Language Models
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gradient-based transferable adversarial attacks achieve state-of-the-art attack success rates against black-box vision-language models (VLMs). However, they require hundreds of costly optimization steps for each image pair. One possible reason is that these attacks typically start from random perturbations that contain no information about the source or target image. In this work, we study whether amortized adversarial generation can provide better initializations for gradient-based attacks. By learning across many image pairs, amortization allows a generator to produce adversarial perturbations for new inputs without optimizing each perturbation from scratch. We introduce SPARK, a lightweight looped perturbation generator conditioned on both the source and target images. SPARK repeatedly applies the same network to refine a perturbation, producing effective adversarial attacks in a few forward passes without requiring gradients through surrogate vision encoders at inference time. We show that these perturbations provide effective warm starts for existing gradient-based attacks, substantially improving attack success rates while reducing the number of optimization steps required. These improvements generalize across different attack methods, VLMs, and unseen image categories. SPARK also produces effective standalone attacks at a fraction of the computational cost of gradient-based optimization. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/Patchwork53/SPARK.

articles.title: Anatomy-Aware Pseudo-Labels and Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff Supervision for Semi-Supervised Pancreas Segmentation
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Confidence-gated co-training assumes that pseudo-label errors are uncertain and concentrated at organ boundaries. We argue that for pancreas CT, where the target organ is a single connected structure and detached fragments are anatomically implausible, the dominant failures arise at three levels: where the organ is, what its boundary should look like, and how a correct boundary is penalized. Anatomical Rectification relabels implausible fragments of a teacher prediction as confident background, without adding any loss or parameter; an audit confirms that its rejections are overwhelmingly detached hallucinations and that thin, tail-like slices are not eroded. Boundary Grafting transplants labelled surface regions with their annotation into unlabeled volumes, replacing unreliable boundary pseudo-labels with ground truth. The residual error is coherent surface displacement, weakly penalized by permutation-invariant Dice and cross-entropy losses. Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff (HAH) supervision anneals a distance-weighted penalty from an annotation-anchored objective that is convex in the prediction to a Hausdorff surrogate, admitting the prediction-dependent distance term only after the predicted surface becomes reliable. On NIH pancreas CT, under the standard semi-supervised split, the full method reaches 84.60% Dice and 4.97 voxels 95HD, improving all four metrics over compared methods; on MSD Task07, 78.90% Dice and 4.19 voxels 95HD. articles.title: Recovering What Matters, Transferring Only What Is Reliable: Toward Precise Reference-Based Super-Resolution
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reference-based super-resolution (RefSR) aims to recover missing details from high-quality references. However, existing methods face two fundamental challenges. First, perceptual plausibility does not guarantee content fidelity. Existing methods often produce visually convincing details without faithfully recovering reference-specific information, such as text, codes, and identity cues. Second, faithful reference reading does not guarantee reliable information transfer. Increasing reference utilization also exposes the restoration process to misleading content, as global semantic relevance does not necessarily imply local correspondence consistency. To address these challenges, we propose PreciseRef, a reference-aware generative framework for faithful and reliable RefSR. At its core, Asymmetric Twin-Attention (ATA) allows target and reference images to participate in a unified attention space while the reference keeps its own shape. By letting their image tokens interact directly through joint attention, ATA facilitates fine-grained reference information retrieval without explicit image alignment. To ensure reliable information transfer, we introduce Dual-Scale Reference Gating (DRG), which combines Semantic Relevance Gating (SRG) to filter globally irrelevant reference context and Bidirectional Consistency Gating (BCG) to suppress unreliable local correspondences. Furthermore, we establish VeriRef, a benchmark evaluating exact reference-dependent content recovery and robustness to mismatched references. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves 85.6% character accuracy and 76.3% exact code decoding, compared with 17.4% and 0% for existing methods, while effectively suppressing erroneous reference transfer. articles.title: Playfulness as Feedback for Agentic Game Development
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents can generate runnable games from natural-language descriptions. However, a runnable game does not guarantee an excellent gameplay experience for players. In our view, a playful game should provide 1) reliable core functionality, 2) appealing visual design and assets, and 3) rich gameplay that supports exploration and progression. How agents can improve these aspects of playfulness remains underexplored. In our work, we propose Play2Evolve, a recursive game development framework with three stages: Initialization, Refinement, and Evolution. Using playfulness as feedback, agents playtest the game and diagnose issues in its functionality, visual presentation, and gameplay. Their feedback guides bug fixes and asset improvements. It also helps agents propose new gameplay and aesthetic goals for continued game evolution. To enrich game materials, we combine a video generation model with code to create appealing static and dynamic assets and integrate them into interactive gameplay. Finally, Play2Evolve achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods, scoring 60.05 on GameCraft-Bench compared with 50.81 after Game Initialization and 52.46 for Play2Code. Human overall-quality ratings reach 3.67, compared with 2.38 and 2.43, respectively. Our code will be released at https://github.com/showlab/Play2Evolve.

articles.title: FoamSurf: A Voronoi-Surfel Representation for Differentiable Rendering
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scenes inside a scattering medium contain solid surfaces, such as the seabed or rocks, and a semi-transparent medium, such as water, fog, or smoke. Recent Gaussian-based methods produce realistic images of scenes in scattering media, but traces of the medium can remain visible in surface-only renders. Neural fields separate surfaces and medium more accurately, but they are slow to train and difficult to edit. Both approaches evaluate the medium only along camera rays, so its effects along reflected and refracted rays are not modeled. These limitations prevent reliable surface recovery, independent editing of surfaces and the medium, and consistent rendering of inserted objects. We present FoamSurf, a hybrid representation that models surfaces with planar Gaussian surfels and the medium with space-filling Voronoi cells. A single differentiable ray tracer composites both along arbitrary rays, while training priors keep them separate without segmentation masks. Across real underwater scenes, synthetic scenes, and dense fog, FoamSurf achieves image quality on par with the state of the art and the most accurate surface-medium separation among the compared methods. The recovered components can be removed, edited, or stylized independently, and the same reconstruction supports inserted mesh objects with attenuation and scattering along both direct and reflected or refracted rays. Together, these capabilities enable scene restoration, editing, and composition within a single reconstructed model. Project page: https://grzegorzwilczynski.com/foamsurf/

articles.title: OrdiHand-GS: Ordinal-Guided Tracking and Hand-Refined Gaussian Avatars for Digital Signers
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital signers, also known as signing avatars, convey sign language through animated virtual humans, where visual fidelity and linguistic intelligibility hinge primarily on the hands. When one hand crosses over the other, two failure modes dominate. First, monocular expressive-human tracking suffers from ordinal depth ambiguity: either hand can satisfy the same 2D landmarks, and the baseline tracker orders wrists at chance level on 365 annotated overlapping frames from How2Sign. Second, hand appearance remains blurred in neural rendering even after geometry is corrected. We propose OrdiHand-GS to address these errors separately. Relative depth from a video depth estimator and apparent hand size vote, with confidence weighting and abstention, for a front-back relation, which enters expressive-human tracking as a hinge on median hand-surface depth. A source-conditioned residual head then refines the local positions of hand-associated UV Gaussians with the avatar backbone and renderer frozen. We instantiate the framework with GUAVA. Against matched unconstrained refinement, wrist-order accuracy rises from 32.9% to 77.3% at a cost of 0.39 pixels of reprojection error, while a random-sign placebo gives no balanced-accuracy gain. A 2x2 factorial evaluation attributes most of the interaction-rendering improvement to tracking-stage refinement, with a smaller additional benefit from the residual.

articles.title: Streaming Tax: Can Streaming VLMs Replace Their Offline Parents?
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most vision-language models (VLMs) specialize in offline video understanding; in contrast, their post-trained versions, streaming VLMs, can perform live interactions. We investigate whether streaming VLMs can replace their offline parent models on offline tasks. Such replacement could reduce deployment costs and improve efficiency. We propose Streaming Tax to systematically evaluate streaming VLMs on offline tasks. Our exploration spans three core dimensions: understanding, trustworthiness, and generalization across 15 benchmarks. Our findings reveal a critical gap between offline capability preservation and practical replaceability. This gap emerges at two stages: streaming adaptation can alter trustworthy behavior even when offline understanding is largely preserved, while the native streaming protocol can introduce further performance losses. Our analyses show that some of these losses arise from restricted access to historical visual evidence and failures to deliver usable responses. Importantly, regarding safety, streaming models often leave both harmful and legitimate requests unanswered rather than genuinely refusing unsafe ones. We then propose Stream++, a training-free plugin to improve streaming VLMs on offline tasks.

articles.title: EvOrderBench: When do sampled frames establish event order?
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked which of two actions in a video happened first, given only a few sampled frames. Such frames can show that both actions occurred without showing which came first, so a reliable model should state an order only when the frames establish it. Forced-choice temporal benchmarks treat every input as answerable and reward lucky guesses, while answerability benchmarks do not separate frames that miss an action from frames that show both actions but not their order. We introduce EvOrderBench, a real-video benchmark of 579 event families. Each family fixes an episode and a question and varies only the frames: of two four-frame inputs, only one establishes the order, and two six-frame inputs extend the other one with either the frames that resolve the order or frames that do not. Every input is labeled for whether its frames establish each action and their order. Across sixteen open-weight configurations and three closed-source references, the best open models order nearly as accurately as the references when the frames establish the order, but withhold correctly on at most 83% of the inputs where they do not, against at least 90% for every reference; forced-choice accuracy cannot reveal this gap. Open models withhold mainly when the frames show neither action; once the frames show one or both, most of them commit to an order. Thinking narrows the gap, even when it is switched on within a single checkpoint, mainly by separating sufficient from insufficient evidence rather than by making models more cautious overall. Accurate ordering thus does not imply knowing when the frames fall short, and benchmarks should reward withholding alongside ordering.

articles.title: A 3D Simulator for Passive SPAD Imaging
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Passive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras provide short-exposure observations for low-light perception, but collecting task annotations for these sensors remains difficult, and annotated datasets are scarce. We present a 3D simulation pipeline that generates realistic photon detections together with camera-motion and semantic labels, enabling perception models to be trained on synthetic SPAD observations and applied directly to real-world data. The pipeline couples controllable scene geometry and motion with a sensor-informed observation model that accounts for photon shot noise, dark counts, and spatial crosstalk. We evaluate the pipeline through calibrated photon-count comparisons and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across three downstream perception tasks. We show that classifiers trained only on synthetic SPAD data achieve high accuracy on real low-light recordings at illumination levels less than 2 lux, without real-data fine-tuning. Similarly, we apply models trained entirely on simulated camera sweeps to real-world camera-rotation estimation and achieve mean absolute rotation errors of less than 1 degree on real 20-degree and 30-degree sweeps at 0.5 and 5.0 lux, when deployed zero-shot. We additionally train semantic segmentation models on synthetic data with automatically generated dense labels and perform direct inference on real-world low-light recordings; the results further demonstrate the usefulness of synthetic dense supervision for real low-light perception. Our simulator thus provides a practical source of annotated training data for real SPAD perception.

articles.title: Separating Environment and Sensor Shift from Acquisition Protocol in Physical Vision Benchmarks
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33507v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In real-world deployments, vision systems must operate under varying environmental conditions, such as illumination changes. Recent work has explored adaptive sensing strategies that select camera parameters according to the current environment and downstream task to improve task performance. Reliable physical benchmarks are therefore essential for evaluating such strategies. We study ImageNet-ES-Diverse, a physical benchmark that evaluates the adaptive exposure control strategy Lens by recapturing printed ImageNet images under varying illumination conditions. We construct four controlled acquisition pipelines that vary printed-image scale and camera zoom, and conduct a pilot study with directly captured physical objects. We find that the acquisition choices substantially change benchmark difficulty on all downstream baselines. Moreover, the average classification-accuracy advantage of Lens over auto exposure observed on the original benchmark does not persist in either our collected pipelines or real-object pilot study. Oracle exposure selection nevertheless retains substantial gains, indicating remaining potential for sensor control. These findings highlight acquisition protocol as an important factor in physical benchmark evaluation and motivate explicit protocol reporting and evaluation across multiple acquisition setups when assessing adaptive-sensing benefits.

articles.title: ArtLang-4D: Articulation-Aware Dynamic Language Fields from Monocular Videos
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language that describes an articulated object is often about its state: the drawer pulled out the furthest, the door opened halfway, push the drawer all the way in. Existing 3D language fields attach one feature to each point and cannot tell these descriptions apart, and 4D language fields condition on video time, which has no kinematic meaning and cannot be set by a user. We present ArtLang-4D, which reconstructs an articulated object from a single monocular RGB-D video and equips it with a dynamic language field indexed by articulation time t, the normalized state of its joints, instead of video time. The geometry is a canonical triangle field whose triangles follow typed screw joints, discovered from the video without any joint initialization. The language field is supervised by a t-tagged caption bank that describes each part with comparative state phrases in a whitened open-vocabulary text space. A free-form query is answered by maximizing part relevance jointly over parts and states, which returns both the part and the articulation state it describes; a command is then executed by moving only that part along its recovered joint. On the 100 objects of Articulate-100, ArtLang-4D recovers more accurate joints and part geometry than reconstruction and articulation baselines, retrieves the queried state far more reliably than a state-agnostic language field, and executes language commands with lower motion error.

articles.title: AVERT: Anomalous Value Erasure with Response Testing against Visual Prompt Injection
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to visual prompt injection, in which an adversarially perturbed image forces the model to respond with the attacker's chosen content, such as malicious tool calls, website links, or advertisements, sometimes regardless of the user's question. Existing defenses, such as diffusion-based purification and image-token masking, mitigate these attacks at a substantial cost to the model's utility on benign inputs. To address this challenge, we propose AVERT, which removes adversarial feature directions only when the model's answer depends on them. Our key procedures involve identifying anomalous value subspaces and detecting answer dependence. To identify the anomalous value subspace, we compare the statistics of each input's attention-head outputs with those of clean images and extract the directions along which the input deviates the most. We then project out these directions to remove the injected content. Because the same directions also carry benign visual information, we apply the removal only to answers that depend on them, namely answers whose likelihood collapses once the directions are removed or that are as likely under unrelated questions as under the user's question. Against white-box attacks on four VLMs (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA, InternVL2.5) and four injection benchmarks, AVERT lowers average attack success from 86-90% to at most 0.6% while retaining at least 96% of undefended utility averaged over thirteen benchmarks. Its defense-utility F-score ($F_{DU}$), the harmonic mean of attacks stopped and utility retained, is 98.0-99.1 and the highest among all compared defenses on every model.

articles.title: Frame geometry, fascicle extrapolation and leaderboard overfitting in muscle ultrasound
articles.feed_excerpt: arXiv:2611.33539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated readings of pennation angle, fascicle length and muscle thickness from B-mode ultrasound depend on the geometry of the stored frame and on how fascicles that leave the image are extended, and challenge entries add settings chosen on a small public leaderboard. This study measures all three in one entry of the UMUD Challenge, which scored 309 frames from six screen layouts, 103 on a public and 206 on a private leaderboard. The pipeline applies layout-specific values of scale and pixel aspect, resamples each frame to square pixels, segments aponeuroses and fascicle fragments with U-Nets and measures the three readings geometrically; the submitted entry blended its angle and length with public notebooks. Because the score is additive, 65 single-change contrasts from 13 base entries measured each decision on both splits. The primary selected entry scored 0.27608 on the private split, the 69th reported position of 690 teams. Reading every frame with square pixels cost 0.029 public and 0.037 private. Of 20 late-stage corrections, 9 kept the sign of their effect on the private split. An audit of the UMUD expert benchmark found that 26 of its 35 frames share their tissue with training images of both DL_Track_US and the challenge. On the 9 frames with no detected match in either set or orientation, the recipe scored 0.213, two experts against two others 0.218 and DL_Track_US 0.263 (0.209, 0.196 and 0.259 when both raters of a reference pair are required), with no difference established. Frame geometry and the extension rule moved readings as much as the choice of model, and small corrections tuned on about 100 public frames did not carry over.
